[[File:Gerrit Blaauw.jpg|thumb|Gerrit Blaauw]]
'''Gerrit Anne''' "'''Gerry'''" '''Blaauw''' (17 July 1924 – 21 March 2018)<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.mensenlinq.nl/overlijdensberichten/prof-dr-gerrit-anne-blaauw-7741227 |title=Prof. dr. Gerrit Anne Blaauw ✝ 21-03-2018 overlijdensbericht en condoleances |newspaper=Mensenlinq |language=nl |access-date=2018-04-22}}</ref> was a Dutch computer scientist, known as one of the principal designers of the [[IBM]] [[System/360]] line of computers, together with [[Fred Brooks]], [[Gene Amdahl]], and others.<ref name=Unsung>[http://www-set.win.tue.nl/UnsungHeroes/heroes/blaauw.html "Gerrit Blaauw"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724171300/http://www-set.win.tue.nl/UnsungHeroes/heroes/blaauw.html |date=2011-07-24 }} in ''Unsung Heroes in Dutch Computing History'', a website created for the IEEE Computer Society's Web Programming Competition (CHC61), 2007</ref>

== Biography ==
Born in The Hague, Netherlands, Blaauw received his BA from the [[Delft University of Technology]] in 1946. In 1947, Blaauw won an exclusive scholarship funded by IBM Chief Executive Officer [[Thomas J. Watson]]. After an initial year at [[Lafayette College]] in [[Pennsylvania]], Blaauw studied at [[Harvard University]]. He received his MA in 1949 and his PhD in 1952 under supervision of [[Howard Aiken]], inventor of the early Mark I computer. At Harvard, he worked on design of the [[Harvard Mark III|Mark III]] and [[Harvard Mark IV|Mark IV]] computers. Blaauw met [[Fred Brooks]] while he was working for IBM and visited Harvard, where Fred Brooks was then a graduate student.<ref name=Unsung/>

After graduation in 1952, Blaauw returned to the Netherlands where he worked at the [[Mathematical Centre]] on the second [[ARRA (computer)|ARRA computer]]. In 1955 he returned to the United States to work at IBM's [[Poughkeepsie (city), New York|Poughkeepsie]] labs where he worked with Brooks on a number of projects:
* He was a designer on the [[IBM 7030|IBM 7030 STRETCH]] project.
* He worked on the ill-fated [[IBM 8000]] series, and in particular designed a paging system for the IBM 8106 in the 1960-1961 period.<ref>Pugh, op. cit., p. 740 note 197</ref>
* He was a key engineer on the IBM [[System/360]] project, announced in 1964. Among other contributions, Blaauw made the successful case for an [[Word (computer architecture)#IBM360Row|8-bit]] (as opposed to 6-bit) [[Word (computer architecture)|computer architecture]].
Blaauw also designed a revolutionary address translation system, the "Blaauw Box", which was removed from the original [[System/360]] design, but was later used in IBM's unsuccessful proposal to MIT's [[Project MAC]].<ref>[http://www.multicians.org/thvv/360-67.html ''The IBM 360/67 and CP/CMS''], Tom Van Vleck, 1995, 1997, 2005, 2009</ref> Subsequently, Dynamic Address Translation (DAT) hardware of a somewhat different design was incorporated in the important [[IBM System/360-67]] computer.<ref name=ArdenVM1966>[http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?doid=321312.321313 "Program and Addressing Structure in a Time-Sharing Environment"], B. W. Arden, B. A. Galler, T. C. O'Brien, F. H. Westervelt, ''Journal of the ACM'', v.13 n.1, p.1-16, Jan. 1966</ref> As implemented on the Model 67,<ref name=IBM-S360-67-FuncChar>{{cite book|url=http://www.bitsavers.org/pdf/ibm/360/functional_characteristics/GA27-2719-2_360-67_funcChar.pdf|title=IBM System/360 Model 67 Functional Characteristics|version=Third Edition|date=February 1972|publisher=IBM|id=GA27-2719-2}}</ref> DAT hardware allowed the implementation of some of the first practical [[paging|paged]] [[virtual memory]] systems &ndash; perhaps the first to be commercially successful. The Model 67 was being used in commercial applications by 1968. The earlier Ferranti [[Atlas Computer]] was a seminal platform for paging research, but suffered from well-studied performance issues such as [[thrashing (computer science)|thrashing]].<ref>L.W. Comeau, "CP-40, the Origin of VM/370," ''Proceedings of SEAS AM82'' (September 1982) ''p.'' 40 &ndash; Atlas "didn't work"</ref> Virtual memory address translation capabilities similar to those on the S/360-67 were subsequently included in all models of the [[IBM System/370]] computer line that followed.

After leaving IBM, Blaauw became a computer science professor in the Netherlands. He retired in 1989 as professor emeritus with [[Universiteit Twente]].<ref name=Unsung/> In 1982 he was elected member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |author= |url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/members/3878?set_language=en |title=Gerrit Blauw |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |date= |access-date=26 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305010044/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/members/3878?set_language=en |archive-date=5 March 2016 }}</ref> In 1997 he co-authored ''Computer Architecture: Concepts and Evolution'' with Brooks.<ref>[http://www.informit.com/store/product.aspx?isbn=0201105578 ''Computer Architecture: Concepts and Evolution''], Gerrit A. Blaauw and Frederick P. Brooks, Addison-Wesley Professional, 1264 pp., February 1997, {{ISBN|978-0-201-10557-5}}</ref>

Blaauw died in Utrecht.

Blaauw was a devout Christian who gave particular attention, especially after retirement, to the relationship of science and faith, a topic he explored in a booklet available in English, Dutch and Spanish.
